STEPBible glosses maskil as 'a poem'. I kept the Hebrew term in the gloss with a hedged meaning, because its sense is disputed (skilful, instructive or contemplative song) and it is a technical heading.

agent_notes: STEPBible glosses the verb dikkita as 'you crushed'. The written form with aleph rather than yod (a rare pattern) is noted by Radak and Meiri; I flag it in the notes without building an argument on it. Rahab is identified with Egypt by Rashi, Radak and the Targum (Pharaoh); I present that as a later-attested identification and the sea-monster reading as the plain mythic background.

agent_notes: צָפוֹן may be the common noun 'north' or the mountain Zaphon (Ugaritic Baal's seat, Jebel al-Aqra), which would make the pair 'Zaphon and Amanus/south' a polemical merism. I rendered 'north' and flagged the other reading in the commentary as my own; the commentaries in the packet take it as the compass point.
יָמִין as 'south' is a direction word from facing east (Metzudat David); in v14 the same word is the right hand. I kept 'south' here and 'right hand' there and made the echo visible.

agent_notes: Ketiv/Qere on תָּרוּם: the packet gives the reading (qal 'is lifted up'); Radak says the written form is תרים ('you raise'). Glossed the reading. The sense shifts between 'our horn is lifted' and 'you lift our horn'.
The 'also means ruler' sense of מָגֵן (a shield as a title for kings, as in Ps 47:10) is my own reading and unsourced; the commentaries read מַלְכֵּנוּ as David or the Davidic king.

history.note: [consider] Say that the KJV turns both lamed-possessives into equations. (KJV PS.89.18: "For the LORD is our defence; and the Holy One of Israel is our king.")

agent_notes: לַחֲסִידֶיךָ is plural in the Hebrew ('your faithful ones'); KJV 'thy holy one' (and BBE) is singular. Rashi, Radak and Metzudat David identify the recipient differently (Nathan and Gad; Samuel; Samuel). I kept the plural.
עֵזֶר ('help') is sometimes emended to נֵזֶר ('crown'), which BBE follows. I kept the transmitted text; this is a textual-critical judgment, not a commentary claim.

יַשִּׁא: STEPBible glosses it 'deceive' (נשא I, so BBE 'deceit'); Rashi, Radak, Metzudat David and Metzudat Zion read it as 'exact as a creditor' (נשה, Exod 22:24; Deut 24:10), which KJV, ASV and YLT follow. I chose the creditor reading and corrected the gloss, and noted the deceive reading in the commentary. Meiri gives both.

history.note: [consider] Write 'I will set' in the v26 note. (PS.89.30 literal: "And I will set for ever his seed")

agent_notes: The Targum's 'the kings of the house of Judah' is a narrowing of 'kings of the earth'; not followed.
The Ketiv/Qere mark on אֶשְׁמָר (pos 2) is shown in the packet as Q(k); I glossed the first-person imperfect 'I will keep' and read the following לוֹ as 'for him', as all five English versions do.

The five English versions split on the grammar. KJV/ASV/Webster take 'olam hesed yibbaneh as 'mercy shall be built up for ever', and BBE has 'you have said'. I keep the Hebrew first person 'I have said' and take 'olam as adverbial 'for ever'. Ibn Ezra's argument that 'olam always means time, so 'the world is built by love' is not the sense here, supports this. Malbim and Meiri read 'the world is built by lovingkindness'; I mention it as a possibility only.
Strongs/morph for יֵלֵכוּן ends in Sn (paragogic nun); the packet's '!' marks it. Glossed as an ordinary 'they will walk'.

פקד is rendered 'visit/punish' in the literal layer ('I will visit ... with a rod'), since the same verb in v. 33 is the biblical idiom for a reckoning; Metzudat Zion's reading 'lack, take away' is mentioned but not followed. Malbim's pairing of פשע with the rod and עון with plagues is his own scheme and is not asserted as the Hebrew's.

אפיר (hiphil of פור, 'break, annul') is rare; STEPBible's 'break off' follows the KJV sense 'take utterly away'. Metzudat David's remark that the throne returns 'in the days of the Messiah' is a later reading and was not carried into the commentary.

אִם-לְדָוִד אֲכַזֵּב is an oath formula with the curse suppressed ('if I lie to David [may I be…]'); KJV, ASV and Webster turn it into a plain negative, YLT 'I lie not'. Rendered literally 'if to David I lie' with a bracketed note.

The second colon is ambiguous. 'The witness in the sky' may be the moon (Rashi, Radak, Targum), the sun and moon together (Rashi cites Jer 33:20-21), or God himself as the witness above (a reading some moderns prefer). I kept the Hebrew's openness in the literal layer and followed the moon reading, which the first colon sets up, in the dramatic layer. 'Sky' for שחק follows YLT/ASV rather than KJV 'heaven'.

The 'sevenfold oath' sentence is dropped. Radak is cited only for what he says: the words of the oath stand for ever. The wording that the Hebrew sense is 'bind oneself by an oath' is a standard lexical point (BDB), not my invention.
Targum has 'covenant with Abraham, my chosen' where the Hebrew has no Abraham; I mention it in the commentary as an interpretive reading only, not as a translation.

agent_notes: STEPBible gives lemma נָסָה (H5145) for נִזְרוֹ; the word is נֵזֶר 'consecrated diadem', from the root נזר 'to dedicate, set apart'. I glossed it as 'his consecrated crown'. נֵאַרְתָּה is a hapax: Ibn Ezra, Meiri and Radak tie it to נִאֵר in Lam 2:7 (the sanctuary 'disowned'); I took 'repudiated' with 'spurned/renounced' as the nearby sense, not 'made void' (KJV).

Revised after the reviewer's request: the commentary now names who reads mitaharo how (Radak: merit, his kingship; Ibn Ezra: his sanctuary; Rashi, Meiri, Metzudat Zion: brightness) and attributes the Genesis 49:17 Targum comparison to Radak, Meiri and Metzudat Zion; Rashi is cited only for the Targum's use of 'megar' for the root generally. The form mitaharo occurs only here, so the sense 'brightness' rests on the Exodus 24:10 parallel and the versions; I kept 'his brightness' in the literal layer and mention the alternatives in the commentary. The Hebrew has only the king's brightness and throne; 'the lustre of his rule' in the dramatic layer is an unfolding of 'brightness', not a new fact.

agent_notes: עלומים is a plural of abstraction, 'youthful vigour', not literally 'youth' alone. Whether the verse says the king's reign was cut short (Ibn Ezra, Meiri) or that he was aged before his time (BBE) is a matter of reading; I kept the plain Hebrew 'days of his youth'.

חלד is read here as a noun 'duration of life, world-time' (Metzudat Zion, Ibn Ezra), so 'what is my lifespan'. The Hebrew מֶה־חָלֶד is awkward; KJV 'how short my time is' interprets מה as exclamative. 'Remember' is addressed to God, and the first-person speaker is the psalmist for the whole people (Ibn Ezra) or a Davidide (Radak). Commentaries that read this as spoken by a descendant of David are Radak's own reading, which I cite only for what he says.

The five English versions split on the grammar: KJV and Webster read the second half as a second question ('shall he deliver…?'), YLT as a statement ('He delivereth'), ASV and BBE as a relative clause. I took the yiqtol of yemalLet as a second parallel question-clause continuing 'who is the man who…', since מי גבר governs both verbs ('who… will live and not see death, [who] will deliver…'), as the STEPBible glosses also show.

Revised after the reviewer's request: 'BDB' is removed. The only source kept is Radak on Psalm 89:50 for the oath to David; the remarks on chesed and on the niphal of shava are my own reading, so their sources are empty. The five English versions split on 'where are your former kindnesses' (KJV, ASV, YLT, Webster) versus BBE's 'where is the oath', which turns the second clause into a second question; the Hebrew has one question and then a relative clause, and I follow it.

agent_notes: The word order כָּל־רַבִּים עַמִּים is inverted ('all many peoples'); Radak, Meiri and Metzudat Zion read it as כל עמים רבים. 'Reproach of' is understood from the first clause (KJV and ASV supply it too). שְׂאֵתִי is an infinitive construct with a 1st-person suffix, a form that is irregular and probably a text problem (BHS suggests reading a different form); the speaker suddenly says 'I', after 'your servants'. I did not emend, and rendered the Hebrew as it stands. The KJV 'mighty' for רַבִּים is a stretch; the word is simply 'many'. YLT 'strivings' and BBE 'bitter words' read the noun from a different sense than 'reproach'. I could not source the claim about BHS and left sources empty.

עִקְּבוֹת is read two ways in the packet: 'footprints, footsteps' (KJV, YLT, ASV, BBE) and 'the delay, the heels', from עקב 'heel' as the hindmost part of the foot (Radak, Meiri, Metzudat Zion, Ibn Ezra). I kept 'footprints' in the literal layer and put the delay reading in the commentary and the note. The messianic reading (Rashi, Malbim) is traditional, not the plain sense of the Psalm; 'anointed' here is the Davidic king.

The verse is not part of Psalm 89's own prayer but the closing doxology of Book III of the Psalter (Pss 73–89). Radak and Ibn Ezra record two readings of it (the psalmist, or the editor closing the book); I note the book-ending function, which is the standard critical view, in the commentary as my own reading with no source.

'bivnei elim' is 'sons of gods' in the literal layer. Rashi, Radak, Meiri and Metzudat Zion read the divine beings as angels; Ibn Ezra reads stars. The plain sense for a psalm of this period is the heavenly council. I put the polemical reading in the commentary and did not cite any rabbinic source for it.

Verse 8 is syntactically uncertain: 'rabbah' can modify 'sod' (a great council) or the adverbial sense (greatly), as Ibn Ezra and Meiri argue. I translate 'great' on the council. KJV 'greatly to be feared' takes it adverbially.
